records.name: Castilla y León
records.current_summary:
Castilla y León is the only Spanish autonomous community that has not enacted any regional LGTBI or gender-identity law, a vacuum maintained across multiple legislatures. The PSOE-proposed ley de igualdad real y efectiva de las personas LGTBI+ (registered December 2024) only reached processing on 11 June 2025 after the governing PP abstained and Vox voted alone against; Vox is on record rejecting LGTBI subsidies in the region. The pending law is explicitly framed around stopping the sexilio—the documented exodus of LGBT people, especially young ones, from the region's rural areas to larger cities.

For a transgender visitor the practical effect of the legislative vacuum is the absence of a dedicated regional equality office, no institutional hate-crime observatory, and no region-specific administrative protocol for responding to gender-motivated incidents. National criminal law still applies and no criminal ban or facility restriction exists in Castilla y León, so the severity floor is set by the state. The deviation from the national score (0.88) of approximately −0.07 reflects the sub-national administrative coldness and rural exposure identified in the dossier as Spain's real fault line, not any region-specific criminal threat.

Compared to Madrid (0.84), which at least operated a trans law and an LGTBIfobia law before narrowing them, Castilla y León has never had the framework to narrow; the gap is legislative vacuum versus legislative rollback. Compared to Ceuta and Melilla (0.85), Castilla y León's deviation is larger because its rural geography compounds the absence of any protective infrastructure and because the sexilio pattern is regionally documented, whereas the Ceuta/Melilla finding is statute-book only with no incident evidence.
records.current_localsOnly: The sexilio pattern itself is resident-facing in its essentials (documented exodus of LGBT, especially young, residents to larger cities; no regional equality office, hate-crime observatory or administrative protocol for residents' complaints), while a visitor's exposure stays governed by state law.

sources.claim: Europa Press (Valladolid, 11 Jun 2025): the Cortes de Castilla y León voted to take the PSOE-sponsored LGTBI+ bill into consideration (76 articles) after the PP abstained; the bill answers regional LGBTI+ collectives' long-standing demands.

Salamancahoy (20 Dec 2024): the PSOE parliamentary group registered a bill for real and effective equality of LGTBI+ people in Castilla y León, aiming to end the "sexilio" (out-migration of LGBTI people from the region), one of three bills tabled that week; group leader Tudanca urged fastest possible processing.

Diario de Castilla y Leon (11 Jun 2025): the plenary approved taking the LGTBI equality bill into debate with opposition support except Vox and PP abstention; LGBTI advocates fear the process could stall in committee. Same vote as the Europa Press report, adding civil-society reaction.

records.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Ceuta
records.current_summary: Ceuta, an autonomous city rather than a comunidad autónoma, has no regional LGTBI or gender-identity statute—a framework gap it shares with Melilla and Castilla y León, recorded in the national regional-law inventories as a gap case only. No incident evidence, no enforcement data, and no hate-offence figure separating Ceuta from the national aggregate was retrievable; this is a statute-book gap, explicitly not an incident finding. The city's distinctive religious-demographic composition (Muslim and Hindu minorities under their own autonomous arrangements) and the border-fence crossing environment create a document-and-presentation context different from the rest of Spain, adding modest friction for a visitor whose identity documents do not match presentation. National criminal law and the state-level police (Policía Nacional, Guardia Civil) still operate in Ceuta, so the enforcement floor is unchanged; unlike the Basque Country and Navarra, Ceuta has no regional equality office, LGTBI observatory, or own police force.

sources.claim: Index page of Spain's autonomous-community LGTBI legislation; lists each comunidad's law and states expressly that Ceuta and Melilla have no regional LGTBI statutes of their own and must instead apply the national equality framework and central-government policies.

sources.title: Radiografía de la educación en diversidad LGTBI+ 2025 - FELGTBI+ / Universidad de Salamanca
sources.claim: FELGTBI+'s September 2025 radiography of LGTBI+ policy (prepared with the Universidad de Salamanca) states that 'Asturias, Castilla y León, Ceuta y Melilla son los únicos territorios aún sin una ley específica en materia de promoción de los derechos de las personas LGTBI+' - the only Spanish territories still without a specific law on promotion of LGTBI+ rights - and that a 2020 precedent study had placed Ceuta and Melilla at the tail of trans-student recognition and protection rankings. The report notes June 2025 legislative progress in Castilla y León and Asturias but records no equivalent step for Ceuta or Melilla. This is the primary national-inventory source for the record's claim that Ceuta appears only as a statutory-gap case with no regional LGTBI or gender-identity statute.

sources.title: Arcópoli pide al Gobierno el traslado "urgente" a la Península de los migrantes LGTBI+ que permanecen en Ceuta - Europa Press
sources.claim: Europa Press reported on 17 September 2026 that the LGTBI+ association Arcópoli wrote by letter to the Secretary of State for Migration, Pilar Cancela, demanding the 'urgent' transfer to the peninsula of LGTBI+ migrants remaining in Ceuta after thousands entered irregularly on 30-31 July, calling transfer 'the only effective measure to guarantee their protection and inclusion'. Arcópoli cited the 'extreme vulnerability' of these people, who flee criminalisation and persecution in countries including Morocco, and launched a free remote social, psychological and legal support service for those in Ceuta. This is a dated, Ceuta-specific LGTBI episode that grounds the record's claim that Ceuta's border-fence crossing environment creates a distinct document-and-presentation context for LGTBI visitors and migrants.

records.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Melilla
records.current_summary: Melilla, like Ceuta, is an autonomous city with no regional LGTBI or gender-identity statute — the sole sub-national finding for Melilla is this framework-only gap: no incident evidence, no enforcement data, and no per-city hate-offence figure was retrievable, so the absence of counts is uninformative rather than reassuring. Its religious-demographic composition and border environment parallel Ceuta's, though the crossing friction is less pronounced. National criminal law and the state police still apply; Melilla's reporting infrastructure for gender-motivated incidents is thinner than in the larger communities, and — unlike Madrid or Castilla y León — no regional rollback or opposition pattern is documented: the finding is purely legislative silence.

sources.claim: Index of Spain's regional LGTBI legislation; states expressly that Ceuta and Melilla have no autonomous LGTBI laws and rely on the national framework and central-government equality policies.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Spain - Wikipedia
sources.claim: The national-framework page (in-scope for Melilla because it states the law a visitor there stands under) records that a registry for unmarried same-sex couples was created in the autonomous city of Melilla in 2008 — alongside Ceuta (1998) and all 17 mainland communities — granting unmarried couples benefits the page calls mainly symbolic; that is the only Melilla-specific legal datapoint the page carries, and it is not an LGTBI or gender-identity statute, consistent with this record's legislative-silence finding. The page also documents the framework that applies uniformly in Melilla: same-sex marriage and adoption nationwide since July 2005; hate speech on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity banned since 1995 with crime-law penalty enhancements for such motives; and legal-gender self-determination on documents without surgery or sterilisation since the trans law approved 16 February 2023 (vote 191-60 with 91 abstentions, applying to people over 16). For this record it substantiates the claim that national criminal and equality law and the state police still govern in Melilla, while confirming no regional trans or LGTBI statute exists there.

records.name: Terengganu
records.current_summary:
In May 2025 the Kuala Terengganu authority erected anti-homosexuality warning signboards at several locations, including near youth-frequented areas around a state university; when criticised, a state executive councillor publicly confirmed the installations were deliberate, framing them as a "constant reminder" to steer people away from homosexuality. A prominent transgender activist and, on 14 May 2025, thirteen civil-society organisations led by a national trans-rights group demanded removal, calling the boards discriminatory hate speech.

The state also retains hudud-style penal provisions (2002) that remain inoperative because a federal statute caps the sentences state religious courts may impose — confirmed current in a 2026 review — while discretionary syariah offences and the federal criminal prohibition of same-sex conduct do apply. What visitors meet here is open, ongoing official hostility, without any trans-status-specific criminalisation documented in the surviving sources.

sources.claim: A Terengganu state executive councillor (May 2025) openly confirmed that warning signboards against homosexual practices installed at strategic locations in the state are intended to instil hatred of homosexual acts, saying the state wants people to consider the acts 'dirty, wrong, and to be avoided'. For this record: official state-level endorsement of anti-homosexual messaging — a direct indicator of the hostile official stance a transgender visitor faces in Terengganu.

Thirteen civil-society organisations including Justice for Sisters (May 2025) urged the Kuala Terengganu City Council to remove anti-LGBT signboards, condemning them as discriminatory and a violation of international human rights law; they criticised the Terengganu state executive councillor's defence of the signboards as inciting hatred and discrimination against LGBTQ individuals. For this record: corroborates the official anti-LGBT campaign in Terengganu and documents civil-society pushback with named actors.

freshness_all.fact: Legal analysis still sound: Terengganu's 2002 hudud-qisas provisions remain unenforceable under the federal Act 355 ceiling, while state syariah uqub offences and federal s377 stand. Post-2023 state PAS crackdown rhetoric found only via secondary reports.

records.name: Kedah
records.current_summary:
In October 2020 a private birthday party was raided and 30 transgender women were singled out from the gathering and arrested, while the event's organiser was separately investigated for "encouraging vice". A coalition of Malaysian human-rights organisations publicly protested, identifying a pattern of punishing organisers and allies of trans people rather than only trans people themselves.

The raid's design — isolating trans women as a category from a mixed party — evidences enforcement capacity and willingness aimed at transgender people specifically. The surviving sources date from 2020 and document no later Kedah-specific incident series.

sources.claim: Malay Mail (30 Oct 2020): a coalition of Malaysian human-rights groups expresses concern over the probe of a Kedah event organiser for 'encouraging vice' after a private birthday party was raided and 30 trans women singled out and arrested — highlighting a trend of punishing organisers and allies of transgender persons.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Malaysia - Wikipedia
sources.claim: The page's dedicated Kedah section reports the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kedah Darul Aman) Enactment 2014 (En.18/2014): liwat (sodomy) and musahaqah (lesbian sex) are criminalised under sections 23 and 24, punishable by up to RM5,000 fine, up to 3 years' imprisonment, or up to 6 strokes of whipping (or any combination); a male posing as a woman in public is criminalised under section 26 (up to RM1,000 fine or up to 1 year imprisonment), while female cross-dressing is not; women convicted of musahaqah may additionally be committed to an approved home for up to 6 months under section 52. For this record: Kedah-specific state criminal law covering same-sex conduct and trans male-to-female public presentation, the direct legal risk a trans visitor faces in this state.

records.name: Aguascalientes
records.current_summary:
Aguascalientes sits under Mexico's federal framework: no criminalisation of same-sex conduct or trans presence, and legal gender recognition nationally remains a state-by-state mosaic that courts have pressed legislatures to complete.

The surviving audited sources document no state-level recognition law, no hostile ordinances, and no state-specific enforcement or incident series for Aguascalientes.
records.current_localsOnly: No state legal gender recognition procedure has ever been enacted here (listed by HRW in March 2025 among states that have not reformed at all), and state anti-discrimination protection for sexual orientation and gender identity remains an unpassed initiative (February 2025) - both resident-facing gaps that do not move a visitor's deviation from the national position.

sources.claim: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (HRW blocked the fetch); the underlying Human Rights Watch news feature (31 March 2025) surveys progress and challenges for trans rights in Mexico, including the state-by-state patchwork of legal gender recognition that the country dossier uses to identify the few states that have reformed.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (HRW report PDF not cached); the underlying Human Rights Watch report (March 2024) documents the human-rights cost of the absence of legal gender recognition in Tabasco - the dossier's reference case for how non-reforming states, Aguascalientes among them, leave trans people without any lawful marker procedure.

Guardian global-development report (24 July 2024) on Mexico City making transfemicide a criminal offence - the country dossier uses this reform benchmark to contrast the capital and pioneer states with the non-reforming majority, which includes Aguascalientes.

sources.title: Gender Recognition in Mexico by State | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim: HRW's state-by-state survey of Mexico records that Aguascalientes 'has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people', one of the states still lacking an administrative recognition mechanism. This directly documents the record's claim that no state-level legal gender recognition exists in Aguascalientes under the federal framework.

sources.title: Persisten terapias de conversión y violencia contra personas trans en Aguascalientes: Diversx – La Jornada Aguascalientes
sources.claim: La Jornada Aguascalientes (23 August 2026, Karla Lisseth Avalos García) reports that Diversx Laboratorio Cultural Disidente activists (Alicia Cruz, Kevin Cruz, Hened Musalem) say conversion-therapy operations still run in Aguascalientes under the guise of addiction-treatment annexes despite the legal prohibition, and that a person who escaped one of these spaces arrived at the group last year. They state trans women continue to suffer prejudice-motivated aggression, and cite the ENDISEG survey showing 7.3% of the state's population aged 15+ self-identifies as LGBTI+, the fifth-highest proportion among Mexican states. This is the first state-specific documentation for this record of ongoing anti-trans violence and family rejection in Aguascalientes beyond the absence of a recognition law.

sources.title: Suprema Corte facilita el cambio del género en actas de nacimiento en Aguascalientes - Infobae
sources.claim: Infobae (9 April 2026, Joshua Espinosa) reports that Mexico's Supreme Court, in Amparo en Revisión 430/2025 with a project by Minister Giovanni Figueroa Mejía, ruled that Aguascalientes' Civil Code requirements for gender change of birth certificates - judicial or ministerial intervention, civil trials, probative proof of identity and marginal annotations - are discriminatory and violate privacy, ordering the state's Civil Registry to grant recognition through a simple, confidential administrative procedure honoring self-perception, with a new birth certificate issued and no marginal notes revealing a prior gender. The ruling's immediate effect is limited to persons represented by the civil association that filed the amparo. This is a dated, state-specific legal development that changes the record's 'no state-level recognition' picture by adding a court-ordered administrative route in Aguascalientes.

records.name: Baja California Sur
records.current_summary: No criminalisation of trans presence. The state congress created an administrative legal gender recognition procedure by Civil Code reform in 2021; after the Supreme Court ruled in June 2023 that excluding children and adolescents was unconstitutional, a 2024 reform expanded the right. Baja California Sur also recognises the transfemicide offence. No region-specific incident or enforcement pattern was found; visitor-facing risk tracks the national baseline.
records.current_localsOnly: The 2021/2024 legal gender recognition reforms and recognition of the transfemicide offence are resident-facing civil-registry and criminal-law machinery.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch state-by-state tracker on legal gender recognition in Mexico (March 2025), covering which of the 32 states have legislated an administrative procedure and the Supreme Court rulings that drove expansion. For Baja California Sur: 2021 Civil Code reform created an administrative legal gender recognition procedure; a 2024 reform expanded it to children and adolescents after the Supreme Court's June 2023 ruling.

Human Rights Watch report 'I Just Want to Contribute to Society' (6 March 2024) on Tabasco: no legal gender recognition procedure there exposes trans people to institutional mistreatment - the August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gomez remained unsolved, hate-motivation provisions are absent from Tabasco's criminal code, and healthcare staff routinely out patients by calling legal names. Baseline for how a non-reforming state behaves.

Guardian report (24 July 2024) on Mexico City making transfemicide a crime with sentences up to 70 years (the 'Paola Buenrostro law', approved 18 July 2024), in one of Latin America's deadliest settings for trans people; over 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022.

sources.title: Gender Recognition in Mexico by State | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim: Human Rights Watch's per-state table states that Baja California Sur's congress passed a reform in 2021 modifying the Civil Code to create an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition; in June 2023 Mexico's Supreme Court ruled that it was unconstitutional to exclude children and adolescents from accessing that procedure; and in 2024 the state congress passed a further reform amending the Civil Code and expanding legal gender recognition to children, adolescents and non-binary people. This is the jurisdiction-specific legal history the record's summary asserts, with the same reform years and Supreme Court trigger.

sources.title: Baja California Sur reconoce la identidad de género de infancias trans y no binarias – El Financiero
sources.claim: El Financiero reports (Gilberto Santisteban, 27 June 2024) that the Baja California Sur state congress approved a reform to the state Civil Code allowing minors to change their gender and chosen name on birth certificates, with administrative processes described as rapid, free and free of prejudice for trans and non-binary children; the XVI Legislature worked the dictamen on the order of the Supreme Court, the June 2023 ruling that had struck down the adult-only limit. This directly corroborates the record's 2024-reform claim for Baja California Sur.

records.name: Campeche
records.current_summary:
Campeche is among the Mexican states that have embraced the reform direction: its congress passed a 2024 Civil Code reform creating an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, following the national supreme court's rulings pressing states to provide one. Identity documents can therefore be aligned locally without litigation — the single most visitor-relevant legal fact in a country where mismatched documents drive questioning and denials.

Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and no hostile state ordinances or enforcement incidents against trans people appear in the audited sources. National context remains violent for trans people, and other states' transfemicide laws (Mexico City's 2024 statute being the benchmark) frame reform elsewhere; Campeche's own record in the surviving sources is defined by its recognition procedure rather than by documented incidents.
records.current_localsOnly: The 2024 legal gender recognition reform and transfemicide-offence recognition are resident-facing civil-registry and criminal-law machinery.

sources.claim: HRW (31 Mar 2025) Trans Rights in Mexico, state-by-state table: 22 of Mexico's 32 states now have an administrative legal-gender-recognition procedure. Campeche's congress passed a 2024 Civil Code reform creating an administrative legal gender recognition procedure.

The Guardian (24 Jul 2024): Mexico City's congress passed the 'Paola Buenrostro law' making transfemicide a crime punishable by up to 70 years - the second of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise it, galvanised by the 2016 murder of trans sex worker Paola Buenrostro; the law obliges the attorney-general's office to publish statistics on crimes against the LGBTQ+ community.
